summary: This document presents a framework for interconnecting Content Distribution Networks. It gives an overall picture of the problem space and describes how the components relate, covering interfaces and mechanisms for things like request routing, distribution metadata exchange and logging.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine two pizza chains agreeing that either can deliver for the other. This RFC sketches the pieces they need so their delivery systems can work together.

subtitle: The big-picture framework for letting one content delivery network hand work to another: five interfaces and how they fit together.

tldr.problem: A content delivery network (CDN) can serve only the users and places it covers. To reach more of them, CDNs need a common way to hand requests, content, rules and logs to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a reference model with an Upstream CDN, a Downstream CDN and five interfaces (Control, Footprint and Capabilities, Request Routing Redirection, Metadata and Logging), then shows how redirection, content acquisition and purging could work across them.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework: it outlines what each interface must accomplish and leaves the detailed specifications to other documents. Together with RFC 6707 it obsoletes RFC 3466.

today: RFC 7336 is Informational. It obsoletes RFC 3466, in combination with RFC 6707, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Terminology
sections.content:
RFC 7336 gives an overview of the components needed to interconnect Content Distribution Networks (CDNs), building on the problem statement and use cases in RFC 6770 and RFC 6707. It describes interfaces and mechanisms in general terms and leaves detailed specifications to other documents. Its many message flow examples are illustrative rather than prescriptive. It obsoletes RFC 3466, which used different terminology and models and was less prescriptive about interfaces.

The RFC adds a few terms of its own. The Upstream CDN (uCDN) is the one with the relationship to the content provider and the Downstream CDN (dCDN) is the one it hands requests to. A CDN-Domain is the hostname at the start of a URL and identifies a set of content served by a given CDN. Redirection can be iterative, where the uCDN redirects to the dCDN's request routing system and lets it decide what happens next, or recursive, where the uCDN first asks the dCDN how it wants the request redirected. Operations are synchronous when they happen while a user request is being served and asynchronous when they happen independently of any request.
sections.plainLanguage: One pizza shop is the one you phoned (upstream), and a friendly shop closer to your house actually delivers (downstream). Both need to use the same words to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Reference Model and Five Interfaces
sections.content:
The reference model has a content service provider (CSP), an Upstream CDN and a Downstream CDN. It splits the Request Routing interface of RFC 6707 into two parts, giving five interfaces in all. Several other links in the model, such as the user agent's requests, are outside the scope of CDNI.

  • Control interface (CI): bootstraps and parameterizes the other interfaces, and includes the 'Trigger interface' operations to pre-position, revalidate and purge metadata and content.
  • Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI): asynchronous exchange of routing information such as the network footprint a CDN serves.
  • Request Routing Redirection interface (RI): synchronous operations to select a delivery CDN or surrogate for a given user request.
  • Metadata interface (MI): conveys metadata that governs delivery, such as geo-blocking directives, availability windows and access control mechanisms.
  • Logging interface (LI): exchange of activity logs, either in real time for monitoring or offline for analytics and billing.

The RFC admits the division between the CI's trigger operations and the MI is somewhat arbitrary. The distinction is what the uCDN knows: a successful status from the dCDN on a CI operation means it has completed, for example content has been purged, while success on the MI means only that the metadata was received and will take effect eventually.
sections.plainLanguage: The two shops need five ways to talk: to set things up, to say where each can deliver, to pass a customer along, to share the rules for each order, and to tally who delivered what.

sections.title: Redirecting Requests: DNS and HTTP
sections.content:
At its core CDNI needs requests to move from one CDN to another. The RFC names two main mechanisms: DNS-based redirection and application-layer redirection such as an HTTP 302 response. Its examples use HTTP.

DNS redirection returns different IP addresses for the same name. It is transparent to the user and answers can be cached, which cuts load on the redirecting CDN's DNS server. The drawbacks are that the authoritative server sees only the address of the resolver, not of the user, which can hurt location-based selection, and that a resolver which ignores the TTL may send users to the dCDN without passing through the uCDN. It can be done simply, by returning an address from a set, or with a CNAME that sends the resolver to a new name.

HTTP redirection uses responses such as 302 or 307 carrying a new URL. The client's own address is known and request attributes such as content type or user agent are visible. The costs are that it can affect application behavior (browsers will not send cookies to a different domain) and that redirections are not cached, so every one reaches the uCDN.
sections.plainLanguage: You can redirect a customer in two ways: by giving them a different street address when they ask where you are, or by telling them at the door to go next door.

sections.title: A Walk Through CDNI Operation
sections.content:
Section 3 follows a content item through a pair of interconnected CDNs, in the RFC's own words a 'day in the life'. Not every operation appears in every flow, and the order can vary.

Before any request, the dCDN advertises its footprint with the FCI and the uCDN pre-positions metadata with the MI. When a user's request reaches the uCDN, it may use the RI to ask the dCDN whether it is a suitable target, then redirects the user with a DNS or HTTP response. The user agent asks the dCDN, which may fetch metadata synchronously and, if the content is not cached, acquire it from the uCDN before delivering it. Later the uCDN may use the CI to have the dCDN purge the content, and the dCDN can report deliveries to the uCDN through the LI.

The later examples cover iterative and recursive HTTP redirection, iterative DNS redirection, footprint discovery, content removal, pre-positioned acquisition, asynchronous and synchronous metadata and multiple upstream CDNs. The framework also treats HTTP Adaptive Streaming as a concern across the interfaces: by default each chunk is handled as an independent content item, and optional identifiers can tie chunks together for logging and purging. Content URIs may also be rewritten at each hop, and the URI used between a given pair of CDNs, the 'ud-URI', is the shared handle for all their CDNI communication.
sections.plainLanguage: The shop first tells its partner where it can deliver and what the rules are. Then when an order comes in, it points the customer to the partner, who gets the pizza recipe if needed and delivers.

sections.title: Deployment Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes deployment models as possibilities, not an exhaustive list. Although the reference model shows every function on each side, a deployment can involve any subset of the functions and therefore only the relevant subset of CDNI interfaces.

Upstream and Downstream describe a specific content item and transaction, not a fixed role. A CDN may be upstream for some transactions and downstream for others, depending on factors such as where the requesting client is and which content was asked for. From the simple one-way pairing, any arbitrary meshing of CDNs can be built, though the RFC notes that support for arbitrary meshing may or may not be in the initial scope of the working group. Other models in the RFC include a CSP combined with a CDN, a CSP using the CDNI Request Routing interface, and CDN federations and CDN exchanges.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every pizza shop needs every kind of agreement. Some only share delivery areas, and some share almost everything.

sections.title: Trust, Privacy and Security
sections.content:
CDNI raises the issue of transitive trust. A CDN that a CSP trusts can outsource delivery to another CDN, which may outsource again. The top-level CDN stays responsible for meeting the CSP's requirements. The RFC assumes a uCDN will trust a dCDN but verify its behavior and take corrective action, possibly ending the relationship. It also says better tools will be needed to identify which CDN in a chain is at fault.

On privacy, interconnection does not necessarily let any CDN gather more about a user, but it makes it easier to share that data with more parties, for instance through the Logging interface. The RFC says the interface documents must include appropriate privacy and confidentiality mechanisms.

On security, the RFC says all CDNI interfaces must be able to operate securely over insecure IP networks, citing RFC 7337, and expects to reuse the security mechanisms of protocols such as HTTP. Existing access controls like geo-blocking, time-of-day limits and URI signing must keep working. Each peer CDN must also avoid becoming an 'open proxy' for a malicious CSP. Two approaches are a signed token in each URL routed to a dCDN, or an advertised set of CDN-Domains that the dCDN checks. Digital rights management is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If your partner shop hires another shop, you still have to trust that the pizza arrives hot and nobody peeks at your customers' orders. So you check up on them.

items.title: Control (CI)
items.text: Bootstraps other interfaces; pre-position, revalidate and purge.

items.title: Footprint and Capabilities (FCI)
items.text: Asynchronous routing information such as the footprint a CDN serves.

items.title: Request Routing Redirection (RI)
items.text: Synchronous selection of a delivery CDN or surrogate for a request.

items.title: Metadata (MI)
items.text: Rules that govern delivery, such as geo-blocking and availability windows.

items.title: Logging (LI)
items.text: Real-time and offline exchange of activity logs.

messages.label: MI pre-positioning
messages.note: Metadata made available ahead of requests.

messages.label: CONTENT REQUEST REDIRECTION
messages.note: A DNS or HTTP response; the uCDN may first ask the dCDN via the RI.

messages.label: ACQUISITION REQUEST
messages.note: Only if the content is not already cached.
